extracted.intended_audience: Voters and policymakers (People of the State of New York); general educated public considering the merits of a proposed federal Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the strengths and weaknesses of confederacies versus a more consolidated federal government, using historical examples to identify design features that promote or undermine union, security, and good administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative likelihood of state encroachment on national authority
rubrics_metrics.description: It will always be far more easy for the State governments to encroach upon the national authorities than for the national government to encroach upon the State authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: State governments generally possess greater influence over the people if they administer affairs with uprightness and prudence. Design implication: federal constitutions must anticipate and guard against state encroachment by providing sufficient federal power compatible with liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of proximity/diffusiveness on popular attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Public affections are commonly weak in proportion to the distance or diffusiveness of the object; people feel stronger bias toward local governments than toward a distant union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: To foster attachment to the national government, its administration must be sufficiently visible and effective; otherwise local governments will form 'rivulets of influence' that counterbalance or overpower the union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary administration of justice as source of popular obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary administration of criminal and civil justice by State governments is 'the most powerful, most universal, and most attractive source of popular obedience and attachment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because courts and local justice are immediate guardians of life and property, vesting these functions exclusively in subnational governments makes them potent centers of loyalty; federal design should consider allocation of judicial functions to shape loyalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility and perceived benefit of national operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations of the national government fall less immediately under observation, and their benefits 'will chiefly be perceived and attended to by speculative men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If national benefits are abstract and diffuse, they are less likely to inspire habitual attachment; practical, visible federal functions increase popular support for the union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent weakness of confederacies without stronger federal organization
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an inherent and intrinsic weakness in all federal/confederate constitutions; too much pains cannot be taken in their organization to give them all the force compatible with liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Grecian Amphictyons, Achaean league, Germanic empire, United Netherlands) show that paper powers without practical force lead to inefficacy, anarchy among members, foreign domination, or dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and appointment method of federal deputies matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal powers administered by deputies appointed wholly by the constituent members, and exercised over them in the same capacities, tend to weakness and corruption (e.g., deputies of the Amphictyons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choice: how representatives are chosen and whether they act as national or state agents affects whether the federal body can act impartially and effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision rules: unanimity causes paralysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements of unanimity (as in some confederacies) make federal action impracticable and cripple the union's ability to respond to emergencies or collect contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice: unanimity often waived or ignored; reliance on it produces delay, coercion, or breakdown. Prefer more practicable voting rules for essential federal powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of common sovereign instruments (treasury, troops, coin, judicature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A durable union requires common marks of sovereignty — common treasury, common troops, common coin, common judicatory — absent which the union is precarious (contrast Swiss cantons who lack these and are weak).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where these common institutions are missing or weak, the confederacy cannot enforce laws, collect revenues, or present a united front in war or diplomacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective enforcement capability vs. nominal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers on paper (oaths, decrees, rights to coerce) are insufficient without realistic means of enforcement; the Amphictyonic council and others possessed formal powers that proved impotent in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design must ensure enforcement mechanisms (troops, fiscal instruments, processes) exist and are not dependent on the goodwill of sovereign members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of power among members and risk of domination
rubrics_metrics.description: In confederacies, the most powerful members often become arbiters and tyrants of the rest (e.g., Athens, Lacedaemonians, Holland), while smaller members become satellites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design should address how to prevent domination by especially powerful members (representation, checks, federal authority) to preserve equity and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to foreign intrigue and intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisions and jealousies among members invite foreign powers to interfere and perpetuate the confederacy's anarchy (e.g., Macedon, Rome, foreign mediation in German affairs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A weaker, divided confederacy is vulnerable; stronger union or protective mechanisms reduce exploitation by external actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediary enforcement structures (circles/districts) often replicate defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments to divide a confederacy into circles or districts to execute laws typically fail because each circle mirrors the same deformities and may either fail or act with devastation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sub-federal enforcement organs cannot substitute for a properly empowered central authority; they risk local abuses or ineffectuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal capacity and fairness of contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements that provinces levy contributions often fail in practice because inland/poor provinces cannot pay equal quotas (as in the United Netherlands); this leads to reimbursing practices, coercion, or collection by force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal fiscal arrangements must account for unequal capacities and provide practicable, enforceable assessment and collection mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and practicability of wartime decision-making and military readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Military preparations in a confederacy are delayed by tedious discussions among jealous sovereigns; by the time the diet decides, enemies may act; standing forces are small, poorly maintained, and locally biased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective national defense requires streamlined decision rules, reliable federal forces, and funding mechanisms not subject to paralyzing negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common laws, measures, and institutions promote moderation and reduce turmoil
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Achaean league, common laws, weights, measures, and money, and a stronger general authority tempered local tempests and reduced disorders among members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmonization of fundamental laws and institutions across members can moderate factional violence and foster stability, but only if backed by effective federal institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local government conduct affects federal dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: If nobles or local rulers govern with clemency and justice, they retain fidelity of dependents and may resist central power; tyranny by local elites can, conversely, drive people to support central authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The character of subnational administration influences whether local centers of power become rivals to the union; federal design must consider incentives for just local governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on non-institutional bonds (religion, superstition) is fragile
rubrics_metrics.description: The Amphictyons' reliance on religion and superstition as an engine of federal authority proved insufficient for durable governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Durable unions should rely on enforceable institutions and capacities rather than ephemeral cultural or religious bonds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of confederacies into opposing alliances undermines unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious or factional separations (e.g., Protestant vs Catholic cantons) lead to separate diets and rival foreign alignments, hollowing out the federal diet's authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal frameworks must minimize institutional incentives for split allegiances and foreign alignments that undercut common deliberative bodies.
